feedback: If you say the poles are cold because they are far from the Sun, reconsider: it is the low angle/spread of sunlight at high latitude that matters most.
A good answer states the shared feature of both deserts — very low precipitation — and the difference in temperature.
If daily heavy snow persisted long-term, the place would no longer have low precipitation, so it would stop fitting the desert definition — use that to test your understanding of the rule.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the latitude–sunlight–climate chain and the precipitation definition of a desert in dialogue consolidates the reasoning and surfaces lingering confusions.
learnerActions: Ask and answer questions about why climate zones band the globe and why the poles are cold.
Explain in your own words why the Sahara and central Antarctica are both deserts yet feel completely different.
Respond to the question: 'What if lots of snow suddenly started falling on Antarctica every day — would it still be a desert?'
activities.title: Talk it through with a climatologist

feedback: Full understanding: defines a desert by low precipitation, explains the polar interior as a cold desert where scant snow never melts and accumulates, links climate zones to latitude and sun-angle, and transfers the rule to new hot vs cold desert cases.
Partial: accepts polar deserts and can place zones by latitude, but defines 'desert' loosely or can't say why low precipitation (not cold) is the criterion — restate the rule precisely.
Gap/misconception 'it can't be a desert because deserts are hot and sandy': redefine desert by precipitation and compare annual Antarctic snowfall with Sahara rainfall.
Misconception 'all that ice means it must snow a lot': little snow that never melts builds up over millennia — low input with near-zero loss.
Misconception 'polar cold comes from being far from the Sun': it is the low angle of sunlight at high latitude, not distance; spread-out rays warm less.
activities.intendedInsight: A desert is defined by very low precipitation, not by heat; Antarctica's interior qualifies because scant snow falls and almost never melts, building up over a very long time.
learnerActions: Read: 'A geographer says the middle of Antarctica is one of the biggest DESERTS on Earth, yet it is covered in ice and freezing cold.' Decide whether it can be a desert.
Give your answer, then give the REASON why it counts (or doesn't).
Answer a follow-up: 'So what actually makes somewhere a desert — give the rule in your own words.'
activities.title: How can freezing, icy Antarctica be a desert?
